notes: \cpara{Yoda's line from \textsc{The Empire Strikes Back}, spoken after Luke says ``All right, I'll give it a try'' about raising his ship from the swamp. The next post, ``Use the Try Harder, Luke,'' returns to the scene; its notes give how the scene ends, with Yoda tying Luke's failure to his disbelief.}

\cpara{States the author's first objection to the line: success cannot simply be chosen, and no plan is certain. The post does not withdraw the objection; it later agrees that ``No plan succeeds with infinite certainty.''}

\cpara{Announces the turn. The word ``was'' links to ``The Logical Fallacy of Generalization from Fictional Evidence,'' which reads as the author's own acknowledgement that Yoda is a character in a film.}

\cpara{Introduces the tool the argument uses: talk about a thing is different from talk about the words or beliefs about it. The post calls it elementary and claims nothing new for it. The notes on ``The Quotation is not the Referent'' give its history (Frege, McCarthy).}
\cpara{Sets the default: saying you will do something means making, and carrying out, a plan aimed at it.}
\cpara{Adds that the plan need not be certain. The goal is the flipped switch, not a probability of flipping it. This sets up the contrast the post draws next.}
\cpara{Asks the post's question.}
\cpara{Concedes the ordinary meaning: ``try'' marks the possibility of failure. The post does not deny this. Its argument is about what taking ``trying'' as one's goal does to effort.}

\cpara{States the principle behind the argument, with a hedge (``many-but-not-all''), and gives no evidence for it. Research on goal setting supports a version of it. Locke and Latham (2002), summarizing their studies, report ``a positive, linear function in that the highest or most difficult goals produced the highest levels of effort and performance''; performance leveled off only ``when the limits of ability were reached or when commitment to a highly difficult goal lapsed.''}
\cpara{Draws the corollary: be wary of goals that are too easy to fulfil.}
\cpara{States the premise the rest depends on: trying to do a thing is often much easier than doing it.}
\cpara{Illustrates the premise with two rhetorical questions.}
\cpara{Restates the default meaning in full, as the first half of a sentence that the next paragraph completes.}
\cpara{The central step. If ``flip the switch'' already means trying to flip it, then ``try to flip'' it means trying to have a plan that might work. The goal has moved from the switch to the plan.}
\cpara{An aside: for a self-modifying AI, the post says, the step from trying to trying-to-try should end at ``a reflective equilibrium.'' It sets up the contrast with humans in the next paragraph.}

\cpara{The psychological claim the argument rests on: people who aim at having a plan stop checking that the plan gives the best chance of success, and it is easier to believe one is ``maximizing'' than that one will succeed. The post gives no evidence for it here; the next note gives research that bears on it. The link on ``lost'' goes to ``Lost Purposes,'' on means that outlive their ends.}

\cpara{The conclusion of the first half, with its condition: ``if trying our hardest is all we are trying to do.'' Research on goal setting supports it. Locke and Latham (2002) report meta-analyses in which ``specific, difficult goals consistently led to higher performance than urging people to do their best,'' and explain: ``when people are asked to do their best, they do not do so. This is because do-your-best goals have no external referent and thus are defined idiosyncratically.'' That is close to the post's own account.}
\cpara{An epigraph from Steven Brust's novel \textsc{The Paths of the Dead}: ask what needs to be done, not what you can do. I could not check the wording against the book.}

\cpara{Applies the quotation. Asking what you can do sets the bar at what is convenient: ``the money in your pocket, minus whatever you need for your accustomed lunch.'' The tone is satirical; the target is the excuse that it was the ``best you can do.''}
\cpara{Gives the other question: what needs to be done may exceed your resources, and then you ``must produce it or fail.''}
\cpara{Restates the conclusion in the terms of the switch argument: aiming at having ``maximized your probability of success'' is a lower bar than aiming at success.}
\cpara{A satirical example: a one-dollar lottery ticket as the ``best'' try at a million dollars. The closing question is ironic. The post's objection is to treating what is ``available'' as fixed.}
\cpara{The positive claim: only wanting the real outcome ``above all else'' produces real effort to maximize the chance of it.}

\cpara{Describes how the lower goal is met by self-deception: the first plan counts as optimal, an inferior alternative can be made up to prove it, and whatever you put in counts as all that was ``available''.}

\cpara{The moral, in Yoda's form. As advice it has the support noted above: a definite, hard target does better than ``do your best.'' The same research names a limit. On complex tasks people have not yet learned, a goal set on the outcome can hurt. In an air-traffic-control simulation (Kanfer and Ackerman, 1989), ``having a performance-outcome goal actually interfered with acquiring the knowledge necessary to perform the task. People performed better when they were asked to do their best.'' A specific, difficult learning goal did better than ``do your best'' (Winters and Latham, 1996). Both are reported by Locke and Latham (2002). ``Win, or fail'' is an outcome goal.}
